title: German cities for newcomers: the famous ones and the ones people overlook
description: Berlin, Munich and Hamburg get the attention, but several smaller cities offer better value for people arriving from abroad. A candid comparison.
html:
Ask ten people which German city is best for newcomers and eight will say Berlin. That answer is not wrong, but it is incomplete. The right city depends on what you are coming for: a job in a specific industry, a university, a budget or a lifestyle. Here is how the well-known cities compare, and which lesser-known ones deserve a look.

The big names

Berlin is the most international city in the country, with an English-speaking start-up scene, cheap-ish rents by capital standards and a culture that lets you be whoever you want. The downsides are a housing market that has become brutal and a bureaucracy that struggles with the city's size.

Munich is the economic powerhouse: car makers, engineering firms, insurers and a dense research landscape. Salaries are the highest in Germany, but so are rents, and finding a flat is a project in itself. It is also the safest big city and the closest to the Alps.

Hamburg combines a port economy with media, logistics and a growing tech sector. It is wealthy, green and understated, with a housing market that is tight but less extreme than Munich's.

Frankfurt is small for a financial capital and very international; a third of residents have a foreign passport. Banking, consulting and the airport drive the job market. Rents are high, but the city is compact and well connected.

Düsseldorf is the quiet choice for professionals in fashion, advertising, consulting and trade, with a large Japanese community and a reputation for good living.

The ones people overlook

Leipzig has grown faster than any other large German city in the last decade and still has rents far below the western metros, plus a strong arts scene and a serious university.

Bonn, the former capital, hosts UN agencies, large companies and a top research university, with a small-town feel on the Rhine.

Dresden offers a beautiful historic centre, a well-funded technical university and a semiconductor industry that is hiring.

Karlsruhe and Aachen are engineering towns built around their universities, with employers queuing for graduates and rents that are manageable.

Nuremberg and Erlangen combine a medieval city with a large medical technology and electronics industry.

How to choose

If your job is fixed, the city is fixed. If you are choosing a university, weigh the programme first and the city second; most German universities are good, and a strong department in a smaller town beats an average one in Berlin. If you have a free choice, decide what you cannot live without: international friends, a specific industry, low rent, or mountains. Each of the cities above wins on something and loses on something else.
